extracted.intended_audience: comic writers and scriptwriters (aspiring and practicing)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for constructing comic-book stories: selecting and using narrative structures, managing transitions, timing/pacing, world-building, and character composition to produce effective comics. Focuses on storytelling techniques specific to comics (panels, page-turns, color, dialogue balloons).

rubrics_metrics.name: Story structure — choice and flexibility
rubrics_metrics.description: “Still thus, all these are formal structures... These are all valid boardings... does not have reason for which you must carry through its the story accurately following these steps literally.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structure can be formal or informal; different writers use radically different forms (Eddie Campbell anecdotal, Phil Elliott nonlinear). You may conceive structure first (example: V FOR VENDETTA 'Video' episode) or let idea start the story; do not force an idea to fit a structure or rigidly follow a prescribed sequence — use whatever structure best serves the story.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transitions between scenes
rubrics_metrics.description: “Transition, the movement of a scene for another one, is one of the most intricate and intriguing elements... The problem is to move of a place or a time to another one without making something drastic or unskillful that could compromise the delicate wire of the involvement of the reader with the story.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat transitions as high-risk moments that can 'wake' the reader. Use techniques (overlapping dialogue, image synchronicity, page-turns, color continuity) to create a credibility interval for scene changes; be aware some transitions can be deliberately abrupt if handled elegantly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep reader hypnotically engaged (avoid 'waking' them)
rubrics_metrics.description: “A successful the story of any type must almost be as a hypnosis; you fascinate the reader with its first phrase... An important thing is that the reader has not waked up until you thus wants it, and the transition between the scenes is the weak point of the enchantment.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sequence opening lines, panels and scenes to deepen engagement. Plan transitions and pacing so the reader remains absorbed until the intended emotional or narrative release at the end.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of abrupt transitions as a deliberate device
rubrics_metrics.description: “The transition nor always has that to be soft... some times you can use a very abrupt transition, with such elegance that nobody will go to perceive any breaking in the flow until the moment has passed... Hitchcock in 'The Birds' example.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Abrupt cuts can heighten surprise or pleasure if they exploit the reader's expectations (e.g., sound cut to image). Adapt cinematic techniques where appropriate, but mind medium differences (e.g., onomatopoeia in comics).

rubrics_metrics.name: Page as unit and page-turn as compass
rubrics_metrics.description: “Thing that I finish making that it facilitates the transition... is to write having as basic idea the page, in way that the action of the reader to turn the page if becomes the 'compass' in which I moves of scene without disturbing the rhythm of the story.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compose scenes with the physical page in mind so the act of turning becomes a transition tool. Use page breaks to time reveals, beats and scene shifts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Overlapping dialogue and image synchronicity for transitions
rubrics_metrics.description: “One that I have used in excess... is the use of the overlapping or coincidence of dialogues... Another boarding is to vary the technique of overlapping of dialogues and to use the sincronicidade of the image more than words...”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Overlap dialogue across panels/pages or align images so conversations bridge cuts, smoothing transitions and maintaining flow. Favor visual continuity when possible rather than expository captions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of color and visual motifs to carry transitions
rubrics_metrics.description: “It is even though possible to use the color to move of scene: the end of a scene... shining red blood... The following picture could, suddenly, cut for... a tent of a florist with a vast profusion of red flowers... the simple maintenance of the red color probably is enough successfully to lead the reader to the transition.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ color continuity or recurring visual motifs to link disparate scenes and cue readers' emotional or associative responses across cuts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing/spacing/compass — control of reading time per panel
rubrics_metrics.description: “Transitions... can also be considered as part of a general topic on spacing or compass... The way simplest and mechanics to understand timing in the comics are to learn how much a reader spends in one comic before passing to the next one... one comic I contend a standard of 35 words will lead about seven or eight seconds being read... a simple graphical image... takes three seconds.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Estimate reading time by words and image complexity to pace scenes: slow rhythm for thoughtful scenes, fast rhythm for action. Trim words where necessary; use panel density and image complexity to calibrate tempo and suspense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Match rhythm to scene demands
rubrics_metrics.description: “The compass must engage the clutch having the scene in the hand... A thoughtful scene that probably demands attention would function better with a completely slow rhythm. A scene of fast action... would function better when how much possible so fast moving itself.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adjust panel count, visual detail and dialogue density to the intended tempo: long lingering panels for contemplation, rapid sequences for kinetic action. Experiment with rhythm to achieve desired emotional effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use quiet scenes strategically to extend suspense
rubrics_metrics.description: “It plays with quiet scenes and it sees as they can be used to extender the suspense moment until strengthening the impact, if necessary.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interleave quiet, detail-rich panels to prolong tension before a payoff. Quietness can enhance the impact of subsequent action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not over-rely on exposition captions/dialogue
rubrics_metrics.description: “The way most obvious of if making this are to explain the expository bases of its world to the readers through legends with text or dialogues, being this also, in my opinion, the less efficient method most artificial and least efficient... It is also the method most easy, being therefore applied with as much frequency.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer showing world-building through incidental details, props, background broadcasts, product names, or behavior rather than explicit exposition; heavy captioning feels artificial.

rubrics_metrics.name: World-building: internalize the setting in detail
rubrics_metrics.description: “The best way, me seems, is first to consider the environment with that you are working as a whole, in detail, before starting to write... I gathered an enormous amount of information on that world and its inhabitants, many of which never will be shown in the comics... What it is important is that the scriptwriter must clearly have a picture of the imaginary world in all its details inside of the head all the time.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Research and imagine the full culture, technology, politics, economy, dress, laws and daily life of your setting so you can drop convincing, trivial details into the narrative without explicit exposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Convey atmosphere/emotional reality of place
rubrics_metrics.description: “Of course... is not only the physical reality of the place that must be understood, but also its atmosphere — the emotional reality... The way that you choose to treat the way that goes to all modify the character of the story and is so important how much the final effect.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide and portray the emotional tone of the environment (e.g., Gotham as paranoid/decayed vs. carnival playground) because it shapes character behavior and the story's effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Drip trivial details naturally (show not tell)
rubrics_metrics.description: “They are the small details as these that make with that its description of a specific place is realistic and convincing. They can accidentally be dripped in the comics, without ostentation, and will be probably more convincing in the ratio where they will be trivial and irrelevant.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Let background signs, ads, names, local habits and sensory specifics appear casually to build verisimilitude rather than dumping informative text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character composition — avoid fifteen-word summaries
rubrics_metrics.description: “He is obvious that if our necessary personage to be described in fifteen words, you will incline in direction to a personage of fifteen words... almost nobody can be described in fifteen words, at least not in an excellent and significant way.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Resist reducing characters to neat slogans. Develop multiple facets, contradictions and context-specific behavior so characters feel complex and alive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Observe real people for authentic characterization
rubrics_metrics.description: “A logical starting point would be simply to leave and to observe the people... It also considers the structure of the character of the people to its return and its proper personality with the biggest frieza and objectivity that to obtain.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Study gestures, hesitations, speech patterns and mannerisms; incorporate those small, specific traits to convey authenticity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decide degree of authenticity vs stylization
rubrics_metrics.description: “...when writing on the personages in the course of its work, you care degree of and pretension and at the demanded degree of authenticity or estilização with the complete notion of the involved principles will arrive at an adjusted.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose how realistic or stylized characters should be based on story needs. Be deliberate about the balance and maintain internal consistency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use theatrical/actor methods to inhabit characters
rubrics_metrics.description: “I closed the curtains... and try imagine what feel if be of fact the personage... I tried the voice, splitting the teeth and raising the superior lip... To make direction... it seemed necessary to speak very slowly... Finally, I perceived that the accurate voice that it looked was of the type of voice as of Charles Laughton...”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Physically and vocally experiment (posture, gait, voice timbre) to discover how a character moves and speaks; use those discoveries to write believable dialogue and actions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plot as situation plus time, not the sole importance
rubrics_metrics.description: “Plot is the combination environment-personas only with the element added time they. If the combination of environment and personages can be called 'situation', then, plot is a situation seen in four dimensions.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat plot as the temporal unfolding of situation; use it to illuminate characters and theme rather than as an end in itself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trim words and synchronize elements for comedic or dramatic beats
rubrics_metrics.description: “Some intuition on as to trim the words is essential... as much to construct suspense in a dramatic situation, or to synchronize one gag for more circumstances.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Edit dialogue and captions to the minimum needed; align visuals, panel rhythm and text to land jokes or dramatic beats effectively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Know techniques, their applicability, and be ruthless in cutting
rubrics_metrics.description: “Everything that if asks for is that if it thinks on techniques that if are using, understanding what they are and knowing where they are applicable... When tools narrative oppresses the idea... must be scratched out without pity or mercy.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Learn a repertoire of narrative devices, test them against the needs of the story, and remove any that detract from the central idea or rhythm.
